claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high compressive strength from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
Partially replacing Hf in HfMoTaTiZr with Nb will reduce alloy density by several percent.
Partial Hf-to-Nb substitution will preserve high-temperature strength up to approximately 1000 °C.
Partial Hf-to-Nb substitution will preserve near-original room-temperature mechanical properties.
The proposed modified composition is (Hf0.8Nb0.2)MoTaTiZr, corresponding after normalization to approximately Hf16Nb4Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 at%.
Adding Nb in place of Hf reduces the alloy's average atomic mass.
The Nb-substituted alloy will retain a body-centered-cubic solid-solution matrix.
Nb provides solid-solution strengthening in the proposed alloy.
Nb's high melting point helps retain elevated-temperature strength in Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr-family alloys.
Nb has a melting temperature comparable to Hf.
The modified alloy will have a density at least 5% below 10.21 g/cm³.
Yield strength of the modified alloy will differ by less than 10% from HfMoTaTiZr throughout 25–1000 °C.
The hypothesis is applicable only to moderate Hf-to-Nb substitution fractions and testing at or below approximately 1000 °C.
Local segregation or unforeseen phase formation could cause mechanical-property changes larger than predicted.
Refractory high-entropy alloys typically have a BCC crystal structure.
Replacing high-density refractory constituents with lower-density refractory elements, including Nb, has produced lower-density RHEAs with strong elevated-temperature performance.

contradictions.description: The phrase '~20 at% Hf → Nb' suggests replacement of 20 at% of the whole alloy, whereas (Hf0.8Nb0.2)MoTaTiZr replaces only 20% of the original Hf amount, giving about 4 at% Nb after normalization.
The prediction requires at least a 5% density reduction, but the hypothesis is rejected only below 3%, leaving a 3–5% reduction that fails the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
